questions.question: Three agents jointly produce a score, but the team wants to allocate credit by each agent's average marginal contribution. Which method fits?
options: A round-robin speaker schedule
A first-price auction with no submitted bids
Shapley-value attribution across agent orderings
A circuit breaker over tool calls
questions.explanation: Shapley attribution averages each agent’s marginal contribution over possible orderings of coalition members, reducing dependence on who joined first. A first-price auction allocates a slot from bids; it does not compute contribution to shared output.

questions.question: With five bids of 0.82, 0.60, 0.95, 0.45, and 0.77 in a second-price auction, who wins and what do they pay?
options: The 0.77 bidder wins and pays 0.60
The 0.95 bidder wins and pays 0.82
The 0.95 bidder wins and pays 0.95
The 0.82 bidder wins and pays 0.95
questions.explanation: Sorting the bids gives 0.95 as highest and 0.82 as second-highest, so the 0.95 bidder wins and pays 0.82. Paying 0.95 instead is the first-price rule, where the winner pays its own bid.

questions.question: What does the 5-layer agent-economy stack use decentralized identifiers for?
options: A portable identity for reputation across platforms
A guaranteed way to eliminate Sybil attacks
A faster route for LLM token generation
A content schema for typed A2A artifacts
questions.explanation: A DID supplies a durable identifier that can bind reputation across platforms, rather than tying it to one vendor account. The lesson explicitly says this slows Sybil attacks but cannot guarantee they disappear.

questions.question: How does the lesson's simple reputation rule update a score after new work?
options: Copy the highest-scoring peer's reputation
Add every past contribution without any decay
Replace the score with the agent's requested payment
Blend old reputation with verified new quality
questions.explanation: The update blends the previous reputation with verified new quality using the decay factor: alpha preserves history and (1−alpha) weights the latest contribution. Adding every past contribution without decay would let stale performance dominate indefinitely.

questions.question: A decentralized marketplace needs contribution rewards but cannot verify output quality. What limitation does the lesson identify?
options: A second-price auction verifies the content of each answer
Credit attribution becomes unreliable without independent verification
DIDs make quality checks unnecessary
Shapley values will automatically reveal every dishonest agent
questions.explanation: Credit is only as reliable as the independent check of the contribution; without verification, an agent can claim value it did not produce. A second-price auction chooses a winner and payment from bids, but it does not validate answer content.

questions.question: When does the lesson say tokenized agent economics is most applicable?
options: Systems where all agents belong to one internal team
Closed one-shot tasks with no durable identity
Open, long-horizon networks with verifiable outputs
Workflows where nobody can check the result
questions.explanation: Open networks with heterogeneous operators and verifiable contributions can use identity, credit, and settlement over repeated work. A closed internal team can often assign tasks directly, while one-shot work has little time for reputation to accumulate.
